what_it_says: A convert from Islam renounces the whole religion of the Saracens and anathematizes Muhammad, whom they honour as an apostle and prophet of God.
context: The formula is the ritual text for receiving a convert from Islam into the Church, in the first person. It is printed in Migne PG 140 right after the Choniates Book XX chapter, with the editor's note that it comes from Sylburg's 1593/1595 Saracenica. The anathemas then go on to name Muhammad's successors, his paradise and his book; the ritual is anonymous and its date is not secure (the attribution to the 12th century is not checked here).
limits: This is a ritual formula, not an author's treatise; anonymous and of uncertain date (Sylburg's source not opened in this run). The Migne page shows the formula printed with the Choniates chapter, which does not make it Choniates's own text. Its anathema is ritual, not a call to violence. what_it_says: Choniates ridicules the Qur'anic story of the camel of God: he asks how a camel with no father, mother or lineage could give birth, and argues that the story is unfounded.
context: Section 7 of the chapter, in which Choniates goes through the 'chapters' of the Qur'an (the divorce law, the camel, paradise, the table, the cow). The Qur'anic camel story is the she-camel sent to the people of Thamud (cf. Q 7:73, 26:155, 54:27–28, 91:13: mapping not checked against a public-domain Qur'an translation).
limits: Choniates's version of the Qur'anic story is a paraphrase in his own words and in Latin (Migne's translation); the Latin is printed beside the Greek. The mockery ('the camel without genealogy') is a rhetorical attack on a Qur'anic narrative, not on people. The Migne note refers to a remark of Barth. Edessenus in his work against Muhammad, which is cited in the note but was not checked.
stance: own view (author's critique of a Qur'anic narrative, quoting its content)
